name: Selling Guru Graphics
description: Who Guru Graphics serves, what it sells and how: brand identity engagements for enterprise and the public sector, scoped and quoted by proposal.

groups.process: Guru Graphics process stage or deliverable
groups.position: Guru Graphics sales position or call to action
groups.proof: Guru Graphics proof, data or legal rule

cards.subject: The studio's scope
says: covers design and branding only
excludes software, development, hosting and support
means no copy should imply that those services are sold
cards.use: need to describe what the studio sells without overreaching
not: includes hosting and support alongside design

cards.subject: The studio's audience
says: is medium-sized enterprises and public sector organisations
is the reason the offer is built around proposals and procurement
cards.use: decide who the studio's messages and proposals are written for
not: is individual consumers and start-ups

cards.subject: The studio's size
says: is small
means clients deal directly with the people doing the work
cards.use: want to explain what a client gets from working with a small studio
not: means clients are handled by a separate account-management layer

cards.subject: The site hero line
says: reads "We Create Brands"
cards.use: need to quote the home page headline exactly
not: reads "We Build Software"

cards.subject: The site subtitle
says: reads "Brand identity, built as a system"
cards.use: need to quote the line that sits under the studio's name
not: reads "Design in a day"

cards.subject: The headline strengths
says: lists 360° brand programmes, sector-literate teams and procurement-ready
puts procurement-readiness alongside sector knowledge and full-programme delivery
cards.use: need to name the three strengths the home page shows
not: lists low prices, fast turnaround and a free logo

cards.subject: The legal name
says: is GuruGraphics Limited
is registered in England and Wales
cards.use: need the exact name to put on a contract or tender response
not: is a partnership registered in Scotland

cards.subject: The company number
says: was checked against Companies House on 20 September 2026
cards.use: need to give the registered number in supplier documents
not: is left blank until the studio is verified

cards.subject: The incorporation date
says: is 8 June 2012
shows a status of Active in the Companies House check
cards.use: need to state when the company was incorporated

cards.subject: The configured start year
says: is recorded as 2005 in the studio's configuration
does not match the 2012 incorporation of the company
cards.use: notice that two dates in the records disagree before quoting a founding year
not: is the year the company was incorporated

cards.subject: The studio's address
says: is Sunley House, 4 Bedford Park, Croydon CR0 2AP
appears in the footer on every page with the other company details
cards.use: need the studio's postal address for a supplier form
not: is a serviced office in Manchester

cards.subject: The From Vision to Brand process
says: has five steps
begins with brand strategy and ends with brand launch
cards.use: need to walk a buyer through the studio's method end to end
not: has three steps

cards.subject: The Brand Strategy step
says: is step 01 of five
defines positioning, personality, audience, values and brand direction
cards.use: need to explain what happens before any logo is drawn
not: produces the finished stationery

cards.subject: The Visual Identity step
says: is step 02 of five
creates a distinctive logo, colour palette, typography, imagery and visual language
cards.use: need to explain where the logo and palette come from
not: defines the audience and values

cards.subject: The Brand Guidelines step
says: is step 03 of five
builds a clear system that keeps the brand consistent across every platform and communication
cards.use: need to explain how the brand stays consistent after launch
not: introduces the new identity to staff

cards.subject: The Brand Applications step
says: is step 04 of five
translates the identity into real touchpoints from signage and stationery to digital media and presentations
cards.use: need to explain how the identity reaches everyday materials
not: researches the stakeholders

cards.subject: The Brand Launch step
says: is step 05 of five
equips teams with the creative assets and direction to introduce the new identity with confidence
cards.use: need to explain how the client's teams are readied to go live
not: defines brand direction

cards.subject: The brand messaging pillar
says: shapes tone of voice, key messages and story
is one of three pillars alongside strategy and visual identity
cards.use: need to explain which pillar covers how the brand sounds
not: covers colour and typography

cards.subject: The complete identity system promise
says: is a complete brand identity system, not just a logo
cards.use: need to answer a buyer who asks for only a logo
not: is a single logo file

cards.subject: The Brand Identity deliverable
says: covers logo systems, brand colours, typography and visual language
cards.use: need to list what the identity part of the offer contains
not: covers stationery and signage rollout

cards.subject: The Business Assets deliverable
says: covers stationery, templates, presentation assets, digital icons and daily-use applications
cards.use: need to list the everyday working materials a client receives
not: covers logo systems and colour only

cards.subject: The Brand Guidelines deliverable
says: describes how the brand should look, sound and behave across every touchpoint
cards.use: need to list the document that governs use of the brand
not: is a launch kit for each channel

cards.subject: The Rollout and Launch deliverable
says: covers launch assets, channel templates and handover materials
cards.use: need to list what helps a client go live and hand over
not: covers research with stakeholders

cards.subject: The identity concepts
says: number four original routes in Brand Discovery
are followed by revision on the selected route
cards.use: need to say how many concepts a Brand Discovery client sees
not: number twelve routes

cards.subject: The revision rounds
says: number two on the selected route in Brand Discovery
cards.use: need to say how much revision Brand Discovery includes
not: are unlimited until the client is satisfied

cards.subject: The launch kit
says: covers every owned channel in the Rollout Programme
sits alongside an estate, signage and print rollout plan
cards.use: need to say what supports going live across all the client's channels
not: is part of Brand Discovery

cards.subject: Brand Discovery
says: is engagement 01, Foundation
typically takes 3-4 weeks
includes stakeholder and audience research and positioning and brand direction
cards.use: need the smallest of the four engagements
not: typically takes 8-12 weeks

cards.subject: Identity Programme
says: is engagement 02, Identity
typically takes 6-8 weeks
adds complete business stationery, templates and a digital asset library to Brand Discovery
cards.use: need the engagement that adds stationery and templates
not: includes 30-60 page brand guidelines

cards.subject: Brand System
says: is engagement 03, Consistency
typically takes 8-12 weeks
adds 30-60 page brand guidelines, brand voice and accessibility standards to the Identity Programme
cards.use: need the engagement that adds full guidelines and brand voice
not: is scoped per organisation with no typical duration

cards.subject: Rollout Programme
says: is engagement 04, Rollout
is scoped per organisation
adds a launch kit, rollout plan and staff toolkit to the Brand System
cards.use: need the engagement that rolls the brand out across an estate
not: typically takes 3-4 weeks

cards.subject: The engagement ladder
says: makes each engagement include everything in the one before
cards.use: need to explain how the four engagements relate
not: lets a client pick unrelated modules

cards.subject: The typical durations
says: are typical, not promises
should be described to buyers as typical ranges
cards.use: need to avoid promising a delivery time
not: are guaranteed dates

cards.subject: The accessibility standards
says: are included in the Brand System as accessibility and contrast standards
are backed by an accessibility page on the studio's site
cards.use: need to say where accessibility sits in the offer
not: are only available in the Rollout Programme

cards.subject: Request a proposal
says: is the call to action on each engagement
reflects that every engagement is scoped and quoted against the client's own requirements
cards.use: need the button wording that fits proposal-led selling
not: is replaced by Book Now

cards.subject: Start a Conversation
says: is the closing call to action
invites the organisation to say where it is today and where it wants the brand to go
leads to the studio helping choose the right level of identity support
cards.use: need the invitation for an organisation that is not ready to ask for a proposal
not: asks the buyer to choose a fixed package

cards.subject: Fixed-price packages with Book Now
says: were in the supplied design
were deliberately replaced by the studio
are described as a freelance sales motion
cards.use: learn why a template was changed for enterprise buyers
not: suit enterprise and public sector buying

cards.subject: Proposal-led selling
says: matches how enterprise and public sector buyers work through proposals and procurement
puts engagement tiers on the cards instead of prices
cards.use: need to explain why the cards carry tiers rather than fixed packages
not: is a freelance sales motion

cards.subject: Procurement ready
says: is one of the three headline strengths
signals the studio can work through formal buying processes
cards.use: need to tell a buyer the studio can handle formal procurement
not: means the studio holds a public sector framework place

cards.subject: The public sector wording rule
says: avoids the word growth because it reads wrong to a public sector buyer
uses the heading Your Reputation Engine instead
cards.use: write copy for a council or other public body
not: uses the word growth in the headline

cards.subject: Your Reputation Engine
says: is built on trust, recognition, standing apart from peers, and engagement and loyalty
cards.use: need the public sector section's heading and its four supports
not: is built on revenue growth and lead generation

cards.subject: The Who Trusted Us clients wall
says: shows marks of organisations the studio has delivered design or branding work for
carries a note saying what the logos mean and do not mean
cards.use: need to describe what the logos on the home page represent
not: shows organisations that have endorsed the studio

cards.subject: The logo disclaimer
says: says each mark is the property of the organisation it identifies
describes the logos as a record of work, not an endorsement
offers details of any individual engagement on request
cards.use: need to explain why a client's logo appears on the site
not: says the logos are testimonials

cards.subject: Written permission for client marks
says: is needed before showing each client's mark
exists because most large organisations have rules about who may display their logo
cards.use: want to add a client's logo to the clients wall
not: is unnecessary if the studio did the work

cards.subject: The evidence rule
says: says to keep only what you could evidence if asked
cards.use: are tempted to leave an unprovable claim on the site
not: says a claim is safe if no one has queried it

cards.subject: Testimonial integrity
says: requires testimonials to be reproduced exactly as the clients wrote them
treats editing a testimonial as dishonest and, under the DMCC Act 2024, a regulatory problem
cards.use: want to tidy the wording of a client's testimonial
not: allows light editing for length

cards.subject: The credentials page
says: renders a row only when it is filled in
shows on request for the rest
cards.use: need to know how missing supplier details are displayed
not: shows placeholder values until real ones arrive

cards.subject: The empty supplier fields
says: include professional indemnity, public liability and employers' liability cover, Cyber Essentials, D-U-N-S number and any framework or DPS
are empty on purpose until real values are known
cards.use: feel pressure to fill in cover levels before they are confirmed
not: are filled with typical values for the sector

cards.subject: Publishing an unheld credential
says: is the one mistake on the credentials page a procurement team will never forgive
cards.use: consider showing a cover level or certification the studio does not hold
not: is a minor issue that can be corrected after award

cards.subject: The enquiry form
says: processes personal data
tells people what their address is used for and links the policy
cards.use: design or review the form on the contact page
not: is exempt from data protection rules because it is a business site

cards.subject: The newsletter promise
says: is occasional notes on brand identity in the enterprise and public sector, no more than once a month
says the address is used for this newsletter only
lets people unsubscribe from any edition
cards.use: need to state what a newsletter subscriber is promised
not: promises a weekly digest

cards.subject: Informed consent on the form
says: requires the form to say what the address is used for and link the policy
cards.use: need consent that would stand up if challenged
not: is satisfied by a pre-ticked box with no explanation

cards.subject: The registered company details in the footer
says: show registered name, number, place of registration and registered office on every page
follow the Companies Act 2006 s82 and the 2015 regulations
cards.use: need to know what a UK limited company must show on its website
not: are optional for companies that have a contact form

cards.subject: The ideal customer profile
says: describes the type of organisation a supplier serves best
guides which enquiries deserve early effort
cards.use: need to decide which kinds of organisation to prioritise
not: describes one named individual's goals and frustrations

cards.subject: The buyer persona
says: describes a typical individual buyer's role, goals and concerns
shapes how messages are written for that kind of person
cards.use: need to tune a message for a particular type of decision maker
not: lists the industries a supplier should target

cards.subject: BANT
says: is a short qualification checklist covering budget, authority, need and timing
cards.use: want a quick four-question check on a new lead
not: scores a buyer's champion, metrics and economic buyer

cards.subject: MEDDIC
says: qualifies by metrics, economic buyer, decision criteria, decision process, identified pain and champion
suits long, multi-person buying decisions
cards.use: need a fuller framework for a complex sale with many people involved
not: is a four-question checklist on budget and timing

cards.subject: Disqualification
says: ends a pursuit early when fit, need or ability to buy is missing
protects time for better opportunities
cards.use: find that an opportunity has no real need or no route to a decision
not: is a failure to be hidden from the forecast

cards.subject: A trigger event
says: is a change such as a merger, restructure or new leadership that makes action likely
explains why a buyer is acting now
cards.use: ask why this organisation is looking at the problem at this moment
not: is a scheduled marketing email

cards.subject: An inbound enquiry
says: arrives because the buyer reached out first
still needs qualifying before a proposal is written
cards.use: receive a contact form submission from a stranger
not: can be treated as a signed commitment to buy

cards.subject: Lead scoring
says: ranks leads by fit and engagement signals
needs periodic review against which leads actually became clients
cards.use: need to prioritise a large volume of incoming leads
not: replaces the need for any conversation with the buyer

cards.subject: The economic buyer
says: holds authority over the budget
can approve or veto the spend
cards.use: need to find the person who can actually release the money
not: works with the deliverable every day

cards.subject: The champion
says: advocates internally for the supplier
helps by sharing how the organisation decides
cards.use: have a contact inside who wants you to win
not: opposes the purchase in favour of an alternative

cards.subject: The end user
says: works with the deliverable day to day
can reveal practical needs senior sponsors miss
cards.use: need to learn how the finished work will actually be used
not: owns the budget

cards.subject: The gatekeeper
says: controls access to decision makers
may be an assistant or a front-line contact
cards.use: cannot get through to the person who decides
not: signs the contract

cards.subject: The procurement officer
says: runs the formal buying process
enforces the organisation's purchasing rules
cards.use: must follow a mandated route to buy
not: decides the creative direction

cards.subject: The legal reviewer
says: checks contract terms and data protection obligations
can add weeks if contract points are raised late
cards.use: need to expect scrutiny of terms and liability
not: scores the creative quality of the bids

cards.subject: The blocker
says: opposes the purchase or prefers an alternative
needs to be understood rather than ignored
cards.use: meet a stakeholder who raises resistance in every meeting
not: advocates for the supplier inside the organisation

cards.subject: The executive sponsor
says: gives the project senior backing
can clear obstacles that a day-to-day lead cannot
cards.use: need senior cover when a project stalls between departments
not: only processes purchase orders

cards.subject: An open question
says: invites a fuller answer than yes or no
starts with words such as how, what or tell me about
cards.use: want the buyer to describe their situation in their own words
not: confirms a single fact

cards.subject: A closed question
says: confirms a fact with a yes or no answer
is useful for checking details once the picture is clear
cards.use: need to confirm a date, a name or a yes-no detail
not: draws out a long narrative

cards.subject: A probing follow-up
says: digs deeper into the answer just given
shows you listened to the specific words used
cards.use: hear a vague answer and need more detail
not: moves to a new unrelated topic

cards.subject: Summarising back
says: restates what you heard to confirm understanding
gives the buyer a chance to correct you
cards.use: reach the end of a long discovery conversation
not: adds new proposals to the discussion

cards.subject: Laddering
says: moves from a stated need to its consequences and business impact by asking why again
reveals the reason behind a surface request
cards.use: hear a request for something but not why it matters
not: lists competitors' features

cards.subject: An impact question
says: draws out the cost of the problem staying unsolved
cards.use: need to understand what happens if the buyer does nothing
not: asks which supplier the buyer used before

cards.subject: A success-criteria question
says: asks how the buyer will judge the result
turns a vague wish into something checkable
cards.use: need to know how the work will be judged afterwards
not: asks what budget is available

cards.subject: A strategic pause
says: leaves silence after an answer so the buyer adds more
often surfaces the real concern
cards.use: sense the buyer has more to say after a short answer
not: fills the gap with a quick pitch

cards.subject: A scoping assumption
says: states a condition taken as true that the price depends on
protects both sides if the condition turns out to be wrong
cards.use: need to record what the quote relies on
not: lists what is not included

cards.subject: An exclusion
says: states clearly what is not included in the work
prevents later disagreements about what was bought
cards.use: want to spell out what the price does not cover
not: records a condition the price depends on

cards.subject: A deliverable
says: is a tangible output handed over to the client
cards.use: need to name what the client will actually receive
not: is a risk the supplier cannot control

cards.subject: Acceptance criteria
says: are the agreed tests by which a deliverable is judged complete
should be written before work starts
cards.use: need to know when a piece of work counts as finished
not: are a list of client preferences collected after delivery

cards.subject: Change control
says: assesses and agrees changes to scope before the work is done
records the effect of a change on time and cost
cards.use: are asked by a client for something outside the agreed scope
not: lets the team quietly absorb extra requests

cards.subject: Scope creep
says: is growth in the work without a matching change to time or cost
usually builds up through small, informal requests
cards.use: notice small extra requests are adding up with no agreed change
not: is a formal variation agreed in writing

cards.subject: A dependency
says: is something outside the supplier's control that the work needs
includes client feedback and approvals arriving on time
cards.use: need to flag that the timeline relies on client inputs
not: is an exclusion from the price

cards.subject: A revision limit
says: caps the number of feedback rounds in the agreed work
stops open-ended refinement
cards.use: want to agree how much feedback is included
not: guarantees the client will like the result

cards.subject: A single point of contact
says: is one named client person who consolidates feedback
avoids contradictory comments from many people
cards.use: receive conflicting feedback from several people at the client
not: is the supplier's account manager

cards.subject: The executive summary
says: condenses the problem, the proposed approach and the benefits for busy decision makers
is often the only part a senior reader reaches
cards.use: need the section a senior decision maker will read first
not: lists every assumption and exclusion

cards.subject: The understanding of requirements
says: shows the buyer's situation back in their own terms
cards.use: want the buyer to see you listened
not: lists the supplier's founding history

cards.subject: The approach section
says: explains how the work will be done step by step
cards.use: need to show how the method works in practice
not: gives references from past clients

cards.subject: The team and experience section
says: names who will do the work
shows comparable work done before
cards.use: need to show the buyer who they will actually work with
not: explains the payment schedule

cards.subject: The references section
says: gives independent proof from comparable clients
depends on written permission to name them
cards.use: need evidence from similar clients
not: describes the agreed deliverables

cards.subject: The pricing section
says: presents cost against the defined scope with its assumptions
should make clear what is and is not included
cards.use: need to show what the buyer pays for what
not: describes team qualifications

cards.subject: The risks and mitigations section
says: names what could go wrong and how it will be handled
cards.use: want to show you have thought about delivery risks
not: restates the executive summary

cards.subject: The next steps section
says: names the following action, its owner and its date
cards.use: need to leave the buyer with a clear action
not: lists exclusions

cards.subject: A fixed price
says: sets one total fee for a defined scope
leaves the supplier carrying the risk of misjudged effort
cards.use: scope is clear and the buyer wants cost certainty
not: bills for hours actually worked

cards.subject: Time and materials
says: bills for effort actually spent
leaves the client carrying more of the scope risk
cards.use: scope is uncertain and likely to change
not: fixes the total fee in advance

cards.subject: A retainer
says: reserves ongoing capacity for a regular fee
cards.use: want continuing support rather than a single project
not: bills only on completion of a project

cards.subject: A milestone payment
says: ties an invoice to a completed deliverable
cards.use: want payments to follow progress
not: is paid in full on the first day

cards.subject: A quote validity period
says: limits how long a price stays open for acceptance
cards.use: want the price to lapse if the buyer delays
not: lets the buyer accept at any later time

cards.subject: A statement of work
says: describes particular work, deliverables and schedule under a wider agreement
cards.use: need the document that defines one project under existing terms
not: sets the general legal terms for all future work

cards.subject: A master services agreement
says: sets general terms that cover later pieces of work
lets later projects be agreed with less negotiation
cards.use: expect many projects with the same client
not: describes the deliverables of one project

cards.subject: An intellectual property assignment
says: transfers ownership of created work to the client
is often conditional on payment
cards.use: need to settle who owns the finished designs
not: keeps all rights with the supplier forever

cards.subject: An invitation to tender
says: is a formal request for competing bids against stated requirements
cards.use: face a formal competitive buying process
not: is a quote sent to a known supplier without competition

cards.subject: A framework agreement
says: sets pre-agreed terms so buyers can call off work from approved suppliers
cards.use: see that the buyer can only use suppliers already approved
not: is a one-off contract for a single project

cards.subject: A dynamic purchasing system
says: is a purchasing route that allows suppliers to join during its life
cards.use: learn a buyer is using an open list suppliers can join later
not: closes to new suppliers once it is set up

cards.subject: A call-off
says: is an order placed under a framework agreement
cards.use: see a buyer place work with a supplier already on a framework
not: is an invitation to tender

cards.subject: A selection questionnaire
says: screens a supplier's suitability, such as experience and standing, before bids are scored
cards.use: need to prove suitability early in a bidding process
not: scores the price of final bids

cards.subject: The evaluation criteria
says: are the criteria and weightings bids are scored against
should shape how each answer is written
cards.use: are deciding how to structure answers to a tender
not: are chosen by the bidder

cards.subject: A clarification question
says: is the route for a bidder to ask the buyer to explain requirements
usually has its answer shared with all bidders
cards.use: find an unclear requirement during a tender
not: is a private negotiation with the buyer

cards.subject: Social value
says: is the wider community benefit a buyer weighs in evaluation
cards.use: see a section of the tender asking about local benefit
not: is a discount applied to the final price

cards.subject: Most advantageous tender
says: awards on the best overall mix of criteria, not price alone
cards.use: learn the buyer will not simply pick the lowest bid
not: always means the cheapest bid wins

cards.subject: Equal treatment of bidders
says: means the buyer must treat all bidders fairly and openly
is why individual answers are shared with everyone
cards.use: wonder why the buyer will not give you extra information privately
not: allows buyers to favour known suppliers

cards.subject: Acknowledging the concern
says: shows the buyer was heard without arguing
cards.use: hear a concern and must respond calmly
not: answers the concern with a counter-argument at once

cards.subject: Clarifying the objection
says: asks a question to find what the concern really is
separates the stated reason from the underlying one
cards.use: hear a vague objection such as it is too expensive
not: reaffirms the original pitch

cards.subject: Isolating the objection
says: checks whether this is the only remaining concern
cards.use: want to know whether solving this one point would clear the way
not: tests whether the buyer is serious about the budget

cards.subject: Responding with evidence
says: answers a concern with a relevant example, fact or reference
cards.use: need to resolve a concern about whether the work can be delivered
not: tells the buyer not to worry

cards.subject: Confirming resolution
says: checks that the answer settled the concern before moving on
cards.use: have answered the concern and need to know it worked
not: moves straight to the next point

cards.subject: A brush-off
says: is a polite deflection that hides the real objection
needs gentle probing to uncover the underlying concern
cards.use: hear a vague send me some information with no next step
not: is a firm, specific objection about terms

cards.subject: Reframing to outcomes
says: shifts the discussion from cost to the result the buyer wants
cards.use: face a cost objection that ignores the value of the outcome
not: lowers the price without changing scope

cards.subject: BATNA
says: is the best alternative if the negotiation fails
sets how much leverage each side really has
cards.use: need to know your options if the deal falls through
not: is the first offer you make

cards.subject: The walk-away point
says: is the limit beyond which a deal is worse than no deal
cards.use: need to know the point where you should stop negotiating
not: is the opening offer

cards.subject: Anchoring
says: makes the first stated number influence the rest of the discussion
cards.use: worry that an early figure will set expectations
not: has no effect on the final outcome

cards.subject: A conditional concession
says: offers a concession only in return for something
starts with if you ... then we ...
cards.use: are asked by a buyer for more and want something in return
not: gives a concession freely to build goodwill

cards.subject: Interests behind positions
says: looks at why a party wants something, not just what they say they want
cards.use: meet a buyer stuck on one demand and want to find a way through
not: treats the demanded position as the only thing that matters

cards.subject: Trading scope for price
says: adjusts what is included instead of simply cutting the fee
cards.use: are asked by a buyer for a lower price and want to protect value
not: cuts the price while keeping the whole scope

cards.subject: Splitting the difference
says: meets halfway on a number regardless of the merits
can reward an extreme opening position
cards.use: see a negotiation drift to a midpoint nobody can justify
not: is always the fairest outcome

cards.subject: Stage exit criteria
says: define what must be true before an opportunity moves forward
cards.use: want pipeline stages to mean something consistent
not: are based on how optimistic the salesperson feels

cards.subject: A dated next step
says: records the following action with an owner and a date
keeps an opportunity from drifting
cards.use: end a meeting and need to keep momentum
not: is a vague promise to be in touch

cards.subject: A mutual action plan
says: is a shared plan of steps and dates for both buyer and supplier
cards.use: want to make the buyer's decision process explicit
not: is an internal sales document the buyer does not see

cards.subject: Forecast hygiene
says: keeps the pipeline honest by closing dead opportunities and updating stages
cards.use: see old opportunities inflating the forecast
not: means forecasting only what feels likely

cards.subject: A win-loss review
says: compares why deals were won or lost to improve future bids
cards.use: finish a bid and want to learn from it
not: is carried out only after wins

cards.subject: A stalled opportunity
says: has no buyer activity or agreed next step for a long time
needs a decision to re-engage or close it
cards.use: find an opportunity that has gone silent
not: counts as a strong late-stage deal

cards.subject: Substantiating a claim
says: means being able to evidence a claim if asked
cards.use: want to publish a statement about results
not: is only needed for claims about competitors

cards.subject: Overpromising
says: commits to outcomes or dates beyond what the supplier controls
damages trust when it is missed
cards.use: feel pressure to promise a result to win the deal
not: builds trust by showing confidence

cards.subject: Gifts and hospitality
says: are tightly controlled in public sector buying and should be declined or declared
cards.use: are offered or want to offer a gift during a live procurement
not: are a normal way to win goodwill during a tender

cards.subject: Bribery
says: is offering an inducement to win or keep business
is a criminal offence under the UK Bribery Act 2010
cards.use: see a suggestion to reward an official for a favourable decision
not: is acceptable if it is recorded as a gift

cards.subject: A conflict of interest
says: is a personal or financial link that could affect a decision
should be declared as soon as it is known
cards.use: learn a relative works at the buyer's organisation
not: can be left undisclosed if it is minor

cards.subject: Confidentiality
says: means not sharing a client's information or work without permission
cards.use: want to refer to a past project in a new proposal
not: only applies once a contract is signed

cards.subject: A lawful basis for contact
says: is the legal ground, such as consent, for processing and contacting people
cards.use: plan to add contacts to a marketing list
not: is unnecessary for business email addresses

qa.q: Which of these does GuruGraphics NOT sell?
qa.right: Software, development, hosting or support
wrong: Brand guidelines
Visual identity
Brand rollout
qa.why: The studio does design and branding only, and no copy should imply otherwise.

qa.q: Which organisations does GuruGraphics sell to?
qa.right: Medium-sized enterprises and public sector organisations
wrong: Individual consumers
Start-ups looking for a quick logo
Schools only
qa.why: That is the audience named in the site title and positioning.

qa.q: What is the call to action on each of the four engagement cards?
qa.right: Request a proposal
wrong: Book Now
Buy a package
Start a free trial
qa.why: Every engagement is scoped and quoted against the client's own requirements.

qa.q: What is the main reason a studio qualifies an enquiry before writing a proposal?
qa.right: To avoid spending effort on opportunities that lack fit, need or ability to buy
wrong: To delay the buyer so the price rises
To collect personal details for a newsletter
To prove the buyer cannot afford the work
qa.why: Qualification protects time for opportunities that can actually become work.

qa.q: In the studio's five steps, which comes first?
qa.right: Brand Strategy
wrong: Brand Launch
Visual Identity
Brand Applications
qa.why: Step 01 defines positioning, personality, audience, values and direction.

qa.q: A buyer asks for just a logo. Which promise from the studio's own description is the best response?
qa.right: A complete brand identity system, not just a logo
wrong: A logo in 24 hours
A free logo with any later purchase
A discount for dropping the guidelines
qa.why: The offer is described as a system, with the logo as one part.

qa.q: Which of these is a closed question?
qa.right: Is the launch date fixed for the spring?
wrong: What would success look like for you?
How does your team use the current logo?
Tell me about the last rebrand.
qa.why: It can be answered yes or no; the others invite a fuller explanation.

qa.q: Which proposal section would a busy senior decision maker most likely read first?
qa.right: The executive summary
wrong: The assumptions list
The appendix of references
The terms of payment
qa.why: It condenses the problem, approach and benefits.

qa.q: What is a deliverable?
qa.right: A tangible output handed to the client
wrong: A risk outside the supplier's control
A limit on feedback rounds
A list of what is not included
qa.why: Deliverables are what the client receives, such as artwork or a guidelines document.

qa.q: A public sector buyer sends an invitation to tender. What does that mean?
qa.right: Several suppliers are asked to bid against stated requirements
wrong: A single supplier has already been chosen
The buyer wants a free design sample
The buyer is asking for a framework place
qa.why: It is a formal competitive request.

qa.q: Which person controls the budget in a buying group?
qa.right: The economic buyer
wrong: The end user
The gatekeeper
The influencer
qa.why: The economic buyer can approve or veto spend.

qa.q: Which wording should a public sector section avoid, according to the studio's own copy rules?
qa.right: The word growth
wrong: The word trust
The word reputation
The word recognition
qa.why: The word growth reads wrong to a public sector buyer, so the section is headed Your Reputation Engine.

qa.q: What does each higher GuruGraphics engagement include?
qa.right: Everything in the engagement before it
wrong: Only new items, with earlier ones sold separately
A choice of two earlier items
Nothing from the lower engagement
qa.why: Each tier includes everything in the one before.

qa.q: A buyer asks 'How long does Brand Discovery take?' What is the accurate answer?
qa.right: Typically 3-4 weeks, as a typical range rather than a promise
wrong: Exactly three weeks, guaranteed
Typically 8-12 weeks
It is scoped per organisation, with no typical duration
qa.why: The durations are typical, not promises.

qa.q: Which engagement is described as scoped per organisation?
qa.right: Rollout Programme
wrong: Brand Discovery
Identity Programme
Brand System
qa.why: Only the Rollout Programme has no typical duration and is scoped per organisation.

qa.q: Which engagement adds 30-60 page brand guidelines, brand voice and accessibility standards?
qa.right: Brand System
wrong: Brand Discovery
Identity Programme
Rollout Programme
qa.why: That is the Consistency engagement, 03.

qa.q: Which engagement first hands over editable working files?
qa.right: Identity Programme
wrong: Brand Discovery
Brand System
Rollout Programme
qa.why: The Identity Programme adds editable working files to what Brand Discovery includes.

qa.q: Why did the studio replace the supplied fixed packages and Book Now buttons?
qa.right: Fixed packages are a freelance sales motion, and enterprise and public sector buyers work through proposals and procurement
wrong: Fixed packages were too expensive to produce
The buttons did not match the colour palette
Packages are not allowed on UK websites
qa.why: The change reflects how the target buyers actually buy.

qa.q: What do the client logos on the home page represent?
qa.right: Organisations the studio has delivered design or branding work for, shown as a record of work
wrong: Organisations that endorse the studio
Organisations that have signed a framework with the studio
Organisations that have reviewed the studio's accounts
qa.why: The note says the marks are a record of work, not an endorsement.

qa.q: Under which circumstance can a client's testimonial be edited for length on the site?
qa.right: It cannot; it must be reproduced exactly as the client wrote it
wrong: Whenever it is longer than a paragraph
If the client does not respond to an email
If the edit makes it more positive
qa.why: Editing a testimonial is dishonest and a regulatory problem under the DMCC Act 2024.

qa.q: A client's open-ended answer leaves the real concern unclear. What is the best next move?
qa.right: Ask a probing follow-up on the words they used
wrong: Move to the next question on the list
Tell them what you think the problem is
End the call and send a proposal
qa.why: A probing follow-up digs into the answer just given.

qa.q: What is the difference between an assumption and an exclusion in a proposal?
qa.right: An assumption is a condition the price relies on; an exclusion states what is not included
wrong: An assumption states what is not included; an exclusion is a condition the price relies on
Both are the same and only one is needed
An assumption is a discount; an exclusion is a surcharge
qa.why: They protect the scope in different ways.

qa.q: When is time and materials usually a better fit than a fixed price?
qa.right: When scope is uncertain and likely to change
wrong: When the client wants the lowest possible price
When the scope is fully defined and stable
When the work has no deliverables
qa.why: Fixed price suits clear scope; time and materials suits uncertainty.

qa.q: What does a framework agreement do?
qa.right: Sets pre-agreed terms so buyers can call off work from approved suppliers
wrong: Awards a single project to one supplier
Guarantees a minimum amount of work to every supplier on it
Replaces the need for any buyer approval
qa.why: A framework gives the terms; work is ordered by call-off.

qa.q: Why does a buyer share a bidder's clarification question and answer with all bidders?
qa.right: To treat all bidders equally and openly
wrong: To embarrass the bidder who asked
Because the answer is always wrong
To lower the price
qa.why: Equal treatment is a core principle of public procurement.

qa.q: In a conditional concession, what is the usual pattern?
qa.right: If you do X, then we will do Y
wrong: We will do Y to be friendly
We will do Y now and ask about X later
We will do Y if you tell no one
qa.why: Concessions are traded rather than given away.

qa.q: A next step in a pipeline should be recorded with what?
qa.right: An owner and a date
wrong: A vague promise to follow up
A private note the buyer cannot see
A sales target for the quarter
qa.why: A dated, owned next step keeps momentum.

qa.q: When a bidder cannot answer a tender question within the word limit, what is the safest course?
qa.right: Prioritise the key points and stay within the limit
wrong: Exceed the limit if the content is strong
Skip the question
Attach an unrequested appendix
qa.why: Non-compliant answers risk rejection or lower scores.

qa.q: What should a quote validity period do?
qa.right: Limit how long a price stays open for acceptance
wrong: Guarantee the price forever
Replace payment terms
Define who owns the work
qa.why: It stops an old price being accepted long after conditions change.

qa.q: A procurement team asks for evidence of public liability cover and the studio's field for it is empty. What does the studio's own policy say to do?
qa.right: Leave it empty or show on request until a real value is known, rather than publish a cover level it does not hold
wrong: Fill in a typical level for a studio of this size
Copy the figure from a competitor's page
Put in the highest level to look strong
qa.why: Publishing a cover level or certification not held is the one mistake a procurement team will never forgive.

qa.q: A team member wants to add a new client logo to the clients wall because the work is finished. What should happen first?
qa.right: Get written permission to show the mark
wrong: Add it, since the studio did the work
Add it with a note that it is an endorsement
Add it after the first newsletter
qa.why: Many large organisations restrict who may display their logo.

qa.q: A form collects an email address for the newsletter. Which wording best meets the studio's consent rule?
qa.right: We use your address for this newsletter only, and you can unsubscribe from any edition
wrong: By submitting you agree to everything
Your address may be shared with partners
We will email you whenever we have news
qa.why: Consent has to be informed, so the form says what the address is used for.

qa.q: A copywriter drafts: 'GuruGraphics builds your site and hosts it for you.' What is wrong with it?
qa.right: The studio does design and branding only, so this implies services it does not sell
wrong: It uses the wrong colour of orange
It does not mention the founding year
It is too short
qa.why: No copy should imply the studio sells development or hosting.

qa.q: A council's brief says it wants to 'drive growth'. How should the studio frame its proposal for them?
qa.right: Use reputation, trust and recognition language, and avoid leading with growth
wrong: Lead with revenue growth targets
Offer a fixed-price package with Book Now
Describe the studio as a hosting provider
qa.why: The public sector framing avoids growth and uses reputation instead.

qa.q: A buyer says 'send me some information' and offers no next step. What is the likely situation?
qa.right: A brush-off that hides the real objection or lack of interest
wrong: A firm commitment to buy
A request for a legal review
A request to close the opportunity
qa.why: Without a dated next step the interest is unverified.

qa.q: A client asks for three extra logo routes mid-project, outside the agreed scope. What is the best response?
qa.right: Explain the effect on time and cost and agree it through change control before starting
wrong: Quietly do the work to keep the client happy
Refuse to speak to them again
Charge double without explanation
qa.why: Change control keeps scope, time and cost aligned.

qa.q: A tender asks bidders to submit questions by a deadline. You find a requirement is ambiguous. What do you do?
qa.right: Submit a clarification question through the official route before the deadline
wrong: Phone the evaluator privately
Assume the most favourable meaning
Wait until after submission
qa.why: The official route keeps the process open and gives everyone the same answer.

qa.q: A contact inside the buyer wants you to win and offers private hints on the other bidders. What should you do?
qa.right: Decline the information about other bidders and keep to the official process
wrong: Use the information and say nothing
Share your price with them in return
Ask them to score your bid directly
qa.why: Using confidential information about rivals breaches fairness and could disqualify you.

qa.q: You learn that your cousin works in the buyer's procurement team. What should you do?
qa.right: Declare it promptly
wrong: Keep it to yourself because it is irrelevant
Ask your cousin to leave the team
Remove the cousin's name from the file
qa.why: Conflicts of interest should be declared as soon as they are known.

qa.q: A stalled opportunity has had no activity for months. What is the best action?
qa.right: Decide whether to re-engage with a clear reason or close it out of the forecast
wrong: Leave it in the forecast in case it returns
Move it to the next stage to look healthy
Delete the notes so no one sees it
qa.why: Honest forecasts need stale deals dealt with.

qa.q: A buyer says 'your price is too high'. What is the best first step?
qa.right: Clarify what they are comparing it to and what they expected to get
wrong: Offer an immediate discount
Explain that the competition is worse
End the conversation
qa.why: The statement is vague; clarifying finds the real concern before any concession.

qa.q: Which proposal approach best protects both sides when the client controls some inputs?
qa.right: List dependencies such as timely feedback in the proposal
wrong: Leave inputs unmentioned
Promise a fixed date regardless
Remove the timeline
qa.why: Dependencies make the client's side of the schedule explicit.

qa.q: A buyer asks for a lower fee on the same scope. Which reply best protects the value of the work?
qa.right: Explain what the scope includes and trade scope or timing for price rather than only cutting the fee
wrong: Cut the fee by an arbitrary amount
Remove the guidelines silently
Claim the price is fixed by law
qa.why: Trading scope for price protects the value of the work.

qa.q: A tender states that the most advantageous tender will win. A colleague suggests dropping the price to the minimum. What is the flaw?
qa.right: Award is on the best overall mix of criteria, so quality and other scored items matter as much as price
wrong: Price is never scored
The lowest price always wins
The buyer will not read the answers
qa.why: Cutting price at the expense of scored criteria can lose points elsewhere.

qa.q: A negotiation is drifting towards splitting the difference on price. What is the risk?
qa.right: The midpoint may reward an extreme opening number and ignore the merits
wrong: It always leads to the fairest outcome
It is prohibited in public sector buying
It ends the relationship
qa.why: Meeting halfway on a number makes the opening position decisive.

qa.q: The studio's configuration records a start year of 2005 but Companies House shows incorporation in 2012. A copywriter wants 'since 2005' on a supplier form. What is the safest approach?
qa.right: Use the verified incorporation facts and do not state a founding year the records do not agree on
wrong: Use 2005 because it sounds more established
Use 2012 and 2005 together
Leave the form blank
qa.why: The notes record the mismatch; unverified claims should not be repeated to a procurement team.

qa.q: A buyer's legal reviewer raises liability terms late in the process. What would have prevented the delay?
qa.right: Raising likely contract and data protection points early with the buyer's contacts
wrong: Hiding the terms until signature
Skipping the contract review
Sending the contract in a larger file
qa.why: Legal review can add weeks when points are raised late.

qa.q: A sales manager wants a forecast that always looks healthy. What practice keeps it honest?
qa.right: Agree stage exit criteria and regularly close or move dead opportunities
wrong: Move every opportunity forward each month
Remove loss reasons
Count enquiries as late-stage deals
qa.why: Hygiene makes the forecast reflect real buyer activity.

qa.q: A buyer demands a very low price opening figure and sets the first number. What effect does anchoring have?
qa.right: It pulls the rest of the discussion towards that figure, so prepare a reasoned response
wrong: It has no influence on later numbers
It forces the supplier to accept
It cancels the validity period
qa.why: Anchors influence later offers even when they are arbitrary.

qa.q: A champion in the buyer organisation leaves part-way through a bid. What is the most useful response?
qa.right: Rebuild coverage by identifying other stakeholders and the economic buyer
wrong: Assume the deal is lost
Continue to contact the former champion
Increase the discount
qa.why: Relying on one contact is fragile; multi-threading protects the deal.

qa.q: A manager wants to publish a logo wall that implies the clients endorse the studio. Which statement best captures the studio's own rule?
qa.right: The marks are a record of work, not an endorsement, and each needs written permission
wrong: Endorsement is implied by any past work
Permission is only needed for public sector clients
A disclaimer is only needed for new clients
qa.why: The studio's note spells out what the logos mean and do not mean, and permission is required.
